703.s: Older brother Teddy and Dexter Gordon watched him as a bedridden mother's child; he played piano and radio as a toddler.
703.q: Yeah. My sister Peggy. She’s passed away now, my sister. She really got me into a lot. My brother, who was, I guess, 15 years older than me, he went to school at Jefferson in Los Angeles. He went to Jeff, and he went to school with Dexter [Gordon]. Dexter was in the marching band. My brother was a…

515.t: Father Armando's band and the kitchen full of musicians

515.q: Yeah. My Dad, Armando, Armando John... I’m Armando Anthony. I like to call myself Armando Antonio, but Antonio is my grandfather’s name. But my dad, Armando, had his own band, Armando Corea and his Orchestra, through the ‘30s—the ‘30s and the early ‘40s. I was born in ‘41. So my first memories with…

515.t: Learning from his father; Italian family roots
515.s: His father wrote out 'Again' for him; neither his father nor uncle studied formally, and his grandfather came from Catanzaro.
515.q: Well, the first studious thing I did on the instrument... My dad was a very kind and gentle instructor, and he wrote out... He was a good arranger. He arranged music for the band. And he wrote out several tunes. This one I remember... The very first one was called “Again.” It was an old standard…

46.t: His father the trumpeter and his mother's love of music
46.s: His father played a little trumpet, his mother loved music and dancing, and he was raised by her after his parents separated.
46.q: Well, my father, he played a little trumpet. I never heard him play anything. I was quite young at that time. Yeah. But I understood that he played a little trumpet, you know, he was a trumpet player. My mother always, she loved music and everything, but she didn't play anything.

189.t: Christmas at home and the toy trumpet
189.s: Big Christmas dinners, a toy trumpet as a toddler, and the household of five including cousin Margie Dickerson.
189.q: We had a big Christmas dinner. We had a Christmas tree. Then we had a lot of toys. And before I started playing trumpet, I always remembered on Christmas I would get a trumpet, a toy trumpet. This was before you really had a real trumpet? Yeah, just before I started school. When I think back about…

918.t: Parenti's family, the Liberty Theater, and Giardina's Millenburg band
918.s: Parenti describes his Italian shoemaker father and siblings, his popularity at the Liberty and triangle theaters, then moves to Millenburg and Ernest Giardina's ragtime band with Emile Christian.
918.q: dolphin street and uh the object in view was that we had uh my father uh being an italian who spoke very little english in those days real broken my mother hardly spoke any english but we had uh uh he had a the european value of working hard morning noon and night with that little shoe uh repairing…

572.t: Hearing music at home and the Mares family band
572.s: As a child he heard family music; Paul Mares's father practised nearby with his father.
572.q: Oh yes! Before I played, well I was a kid and my kid brother, my brother, at least my brother Jules, he played music around the house and my sister, my bop and all. They played, you know, this Paul stuff, the family thing. And incidentally, Paul Mares, a trumpet player at the New Orleans Rhythm…

23.t: Why Rose was asked, his records and growing up around musicians
23.s: He was asked because he had the records and was from New Orleans. His family hired Papa Celestin's band for picnics, so musicians were never exotic to him.
23.q: Well, because I was the only one who knew anything about it. I had a collection of records, for example, that everybody knew.

202.t: Born in the Bronx; family singing and his father's amateur nights
202.s: Born in 1915 in the Bronx, he grew up in a household where everyone sang; his father performed on amateur nights and vaudeville.
202.q: Well see when these questions are asked of me, I don’t know. It seemed — now maybe it was just my household or my family or mother, but when we all got together for anything, like a dinner or a party, we all sang. You know that was the entertainment they sung [sings] “by the old mill stream.” And…

1011.t: Parents' songs, minstrel shows and opinions on today's music
1011.s: The semi-classical duets his parents sang, the 'Yes We Have No Bananas' minstrel show night, and Conniff's view that there has always been great, frivolous and junk music, rap included.
1011.q: It’s rhythm with some story and rhymes and stuff. And music hasn’t changed a lot from what I used to be exposed to.

958.t: His parents, being named Béla and his mother's music
958.s: Fleck's parents split when he was young, he only recently met his father, who named the boys after classical composers. His mother played folk guitar and the family listened to the Beatles.
958.q: I don’t know. I don’t think so. But my father, who — it’s a complicated story, I won’t go into too much except that I only got to meet him and get to know him over the last few years, they split up when I was really young and he named me. They had a deal, if it was

486.t: Family attitudes and sitting in with Stanford East and Don Ewell
486.s: His eccentric family, sitting in with Stanford East's small group and following Don Ewell's Dixieland band.
486.q: Oh well my father was a very creative duck. He was very eccentric and I was well prepared for all the crazy people I was going to be involved with. My whole family is a little bit crazy, except my sister, she was a straight arrow. And my brother went to a place — you probably never heard of — Black…

809.t: The LaBarbera family band in Mount Morris
809.s: Local newspapers covered the family band; his father got the boys going and his mother learned bass to join.
809.q: Yeah, there was quite a — actually the Mount Morris Enterprise was the paper before that. There was two papers. You had the Picket Line Post and the Mount Morris Enterprise had early, really early stuff on us in the 50s. What the Shopper would do is they’d put those little photo sequences in. Like…

1022.s: His mother liked Tom Jones and Andy Williams, his father Broadway show music.
1022.q: Well not jazz music but music was, yeah. Oh sure. My mom loved music, she was into Tom Jones and Andy Williams, and those are two of the great singers. You know now that I’m older I realize that. And my dad was always into show music, Broadway show music he listened to beautiful Broadway show…

346.t: Art from his mother's side, music from his father's side
346.s: Uncles Charles Commodore Carter and Arthur were artists; his father, a singer who lost his voice, urged him to sing and then backed his clarinet and saxophone.

499.t: Five drum sets in the house and his mother at the piano
499.s: His mother accepted the drumming, once playing piano with the brothers on Willow Weep for Me and asking about brushes.
499.q: She was accepting. You know? But one of my favorite moments was when we had five sets going, me and Tony and Eric and Nicholas and my dad, all playing — or actually my dad wasn’t there, he was off in his studio I think, but the four sets of drums were going and my mother was playing piano and we…

352.t: Father the piano salesman and the Kemp Brothers store
352.s: His father sold pianos and his mother records at her family's Kemp Brothers store in Utica, where they met.
352.q: Oh yes. He was into — he was a piano player. He sold pianos at Kemp Brothers in Utica on Genesee Street. And when he met my mother my mother was on the record counter at Kemp Brothers, so that’s how they met and married and he was great. He was always bringing records home and encouraging me to…

500.t: A musical family and parental support
500.s: Her uncle played in the Colorado Symphony and great aunts and uncle played blues; her parents and uncle supported her career.
500.q: Yeah. Basically yes. I have an uncle who played with the Colorado Symphony for over 40 years, and started actually with the San Francisco Symphony. And I had great aunts, two great aunts and a great uncle were musicians and they played the music of the early 1900s, so it was Bessie Smith, Ma…

164.t: Vaudeville parents and early piano playing
164.s: His parents were vaudevillians; his father became a San Diego Union editor, and Smith, an only child, took to the piano.
164.q: No it was kind of fun. At the time, I don’t really remember how I started. I mean my folks tell me that I used to go over to the — they had a little ricca R-I-C-C-A piano. I’ve never seen one since. It was a good little upright. And my folks were in vaudeville. They were both very musical. My dad…

597.t: Family show business, Catskills and backing great singers
597.s: Soloff's show-business parents, humor in playing, and what the Catskills taught him; he loves backing Sinatra and Streisand.
597.q: My father was in show business, and my mother was a violinist in Vaudeville. My father was a dancer and a comedian. And my whole family had a great sense of humor, and what’s left of it has. And I always loved the humor that Dizzy had in his playing, Clark [Terry] has a lot of humor in his playing,…

551.t: Childhood in Chicago: reading, music and culture
551.s: His mother and aunt played piano, the family sang at home, and he heard Grant Park concerts, Metropolitan Opera broadcasts, church and choir, and his dignified family.
551.q: A very, very broad spectrum was at my disposal, where anything that you imagined — and I read a lot, I love to read, you know. When I was a kid particularly I read everything I could get my hands on. I used to read the editorials on maybe three or four newspapers a day. You know, different views of…

144.t: Sister Lizzy raising the children; 'Lizzy's Bounce'; taking a school horn into the Army
144.s: His twelve-year-old sister Lizzy cared for the siblings as their mother lay dying. He wrote 'Lizzy's Bounce' for her, then took a school trombone into the Army and practiced in the latrine near Cannonball's band.
144.q: I named one of my children after him. He tried to play drums, you know? He was in a separate orphanage; they divided us. The three of us, when my mother lay dying in the apartment we had, the oldest person in the house was twelve years old, my sister. She would fix the porridge, the oatmeal, every…

376.t: Playing Ramona at age three and his Socialist father
376.s: Taken to a Ramon Novarro film at three, he came home playing the song; his father was a militant Socialist.
376.q: Well, there was a popular neighborhood in those days, and this neighborhood has changed considerably. But this is when I was three years old. Little Jean. Jean, that’s me playing the accordion. And in Brussels, I could show it to you. We still have the accordion. And on that, when I was three years…

136.t: Her sisters' interests and the musical tastes of her parents
136.s: Only she was a musician; a sister loved opera, another danced, her father studied noh, and school music was all Western.
136.q: My oldest sister‟s name is Hisako [spells it]. The second sister‟s name is Miyoko, who is alive and well, we are very close. And the third sister, it was interesting: my father, like any other Japanese father, uh, man, they always wanted to have a boy. So they got a girl, the next one was a girl,…

65.t: A musical house: singers and orchestras at his mother's birthday
65.s: Popular singers and orchestras such as Maria Teresa Vera, Floro Zorrilla and Antonio Maria Romeu played at family parties.
65.q: Naturally, because my father was a good singer. You know, when I heard Panchito Riset for the first time, I remembered my father; my father had that type of voice, like Panchito Riset, when he was very young; and my house was a musical house because the day of my mother's birthday was a happy thing…
